paras: The lynching of Benjamin Richards was the shooting and burning of a Black farmer by a posse and crowd at Warrenton, Georgia, early on May 2, 1919, after a night-long manhunt in a nearby swamp. Richards, accused of killing his wife, had wounded four white men, among them the sheriff, before he was shot and his body burned before about 300 people. The NAACP cited the case in a telegram to Governor Hugh M. Dorsey on the eve of the National Conference on Lynching.

Richards was described as "a young farmer" in the Baltimore Afro-American and the Chicago Defender. According to the Afro-American, on the afternoon before the lynching he went to the home of his wife, from whom he was said to be divorced, shot her dead, and wounded her sister.

A white man named Gunn, driving past, asked about the trouble, or in the Blade's telling interfered with "insulting remarks", and Richards answered with five shots that missed him. A posse of about a hundred under Sheriff Brinkley found Richards at dusk in woods near town. A Continental Press dispatch in the Defender told it differently: Richards was willing to submit to arrest, but the sheriff opened fire as he came to his door to surrender, and he fled calling to the crowd not to lynch him.

During the night Richards wounded City Clerk Williford in the thigh and the sheriff in the face, and later shot Henry and Louis Baker in the arm in the swamp where he was surrounded. Another sheriff brought bloodhounds, and the posse grew to several hundred. To drive Richards out, the posse poured gasoline into the swamp and set it afire; the Defender added dynamite bombs.

A wire dispatch dated May 2 said his body was riddled with bullets and burned after he surrendered to the posse; the Defender said that as he surrendered at 3 a.m. "five rifles rang out." The Afro-American instead wrote that he held the posse off until his ammunition ran out. According to the Defender, the crowd shot the body again, displayed it at the courthouse, dragged it behind an automobile, cut off the fingers as souvenirs, and burned it on the edge of town before a crowd of 300 on "a day's holiday," in the Afro-American's words.

NAACP secretary John R. Shillady telegraphed Governor Dorsey urging that the lynchers be identified, indicted and tried: "Mob worked in daytime. It should be possible to identify them." No report of an inquest, arrest or trial appears in the coverage. Under the subheading "Scores Leave Town," which follows the Warrenton story, the Defender reported people leaving after threats to burn homes, though the passage names no town.

On May 9 and 10 the Afro-American ran it on its front page as "GEORGIANS LYNCH IN DAYTIME," while the Ohio State Monitor kept the wire's headline, "Body of Wife Murderer First Riddled With Bullets and Afterwards Burned." The Plaindealer headed the same brief "Another for Georgia" and added a note doubting the white press's claim that the white man had merely asked about the trouble.

The Defender's story, "Gasoline and Dynamite Used to Capture Young Farmer," centered on Richards's offers to surrender and the treatment of his body. The Cleveland Advocate's editorial "Remove the Cause" set Black loyalty against the May Day disorders and called the onlookers "THREE HUNDRED WHITE GEORGIA BOLSHEVIKI," and the NAACP telegram ran in the Washington Bee and, garbled, in the Dallas Express.

A Blade News Service story, datelined May 15 and reprinted by the Phoenix Tribune in June, cast Richards as a "prosperous farmer" tired of "indignities and insults," omitted his wife's death, and left him still at large. In July the Richmond Planet listed the case among six burnings of the year in an editorial on President Wilson's appeal against mob rule.

Only the Defender says the sheriff, not Richards, fired first. Accounts of his death differ: shot while resisting (Afro-American), shot after surrendering (wire brief, Defender), or "hanged and shot to death" (Cleveland Advocate, Richmond Planet). Names vary: Benjamin, Benny, "Denny" and "Bennie Richard Neerow" for the victim, and the sheriff and clerk appear as "Brindleigh" and "Whitford" in the Defender.

reader.title: Lynching of Benjamin Richards
bases: A posse and crowd killed Richards, by most accounts after he surrendered, and burned his body before about 300 people; every paper that carried it called it a lynching (A1, A5, A10, A11).

A posse of a hundred that grew to several hundred hunted Richards, accused of killing his wife and wounding whites, shot him (after his surrender, per A5 and A10) and burned his body before 300 people, with no lawful process (A1, A2, A5, A10); the NAACP asked that the lynchers be indicted (A11).

The Afro-American's long account (A1, A2), the wire brief (A3, A10) and the Defender's Continental Press story (A4, A5) agree that Richards was killed by the posse and his body burned at Warrenton, though they differ on details.

accounts.label: Wire report (via Black weeklies)
accounts.gist: Richards, after 'murdering his wife', barricaded himself in a swamp, surrendered to the posse guarding it early on May 2, and his body was riddled with bullets and burned.

accounts.label: Baltimore Afro-American
accounts.gist: A detailed account: he shot his wife and her sister, fired on Gunn, wounded Williford, the sheriff and the Baker boys, held off several hundred men until his ammunition ran out after gasoline was poured into the swamp, was shot, and was burned before 300 on a 'holiday'.

accounts.label: Continental Press (Chicago Defender)
accounts.gist: Richards was willing to submit to arrest but the sheriff fired first; he begged the crowd not to lynch him, surrendered at 3 a.m., was shot by five rifles, and his body was shot again, displayed, dragged, mutilated and burned.

accounts.label: Blade News Service
accounts.gist: A prosperous farmer tired of insults answered Gunn's interference with shots and held off the mob, which set oil afire around the swamp; the story ends with him still at large and does not mention his wife's death.

accounts.label: Black editorials
accounts.gist: The Cleveland Advocate and the Richmond Planet said he was hanged, shot and burned before 300.

framing.detail: The Afro-American headlined 'GEORGIANS LYNCH IN DAYTIME' and said 300 took 'a day's holiday' to be in at the 'killing'.
The Ohio State Monitor ran the wire brief under 'Body of Wife Murderer First Riddled With Bullets and Afterwards Burned'.
The Plaindealer headed the wire brief 'Another for Georgia' and added a note disputing the white press's account of the white man's role.
The Defender's story stressed that Richards tried to surrender and described the mutilation and burning in detail.
The Cleveland Advocate's editorial 'Remove the Cause' called the onlookers 'WHITE GEORGIA BOLSHEVIKI' and set the lynching against charges of Black radicalism.
The Blade News Service story presented Richards as a provoked farmer who gave the mob 'all and more than it wanted', omitting the death of his wife.
The Richmond Planet listed the case among the year's burnings in an editorial on Wilson's appeal against mob rule.
